title: Blog 1: Host Static Websites on Amazon S3 & CloudFront
content:
Hosting Static Websites on Amazon S3: From Basic Deployment to CloudFront & OAC Security 🔗 Published on AWS Study Group Community: View original Facebook post
After completing a modern frontend application using React (or Vue, Angular), the next critical milestone is selecting an optimal deployment architecture that satisfies key engineering requirements: minimal operational cost, high performance, robust security, and seamless scalability.
For Single Page Applications (SPA) consisting exclusively of compiled HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and static assets, provisioning and maintaining dedicated virtual servers (such as VPS or Amazon EC2) or web servers (Nginx/Apache) incurs unnecessary maintenance overhead and financial expense. Amazon S3 combined with Amazon CloudFront represents the industry-standard serverless paradigm for static web hosting.
This article details two primary deployment architectures on AWS:
Direct S3 Static Website Hosting (ideal for rapid prototyping and lab learning). S3 Private Bucket with CloudFront Origin Access Control (OAC) (the mandatory standard for production environments). In addition, we explore key operational patterns: handling client-side SPA routing (resolving 403/404 on page refresh), granular HTTP Cache-Control header tuning, CloudFront cache invalidation strategies, and proactive cost governance.
1. Overview of Amazon S3 and Amazon CloudFront Before implementing the deployment pipelines, it is essential to understand the architectural responsibilities of each AWS service:
Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service): A highly scalable object storage service delivering near-absolute data durability and enterprise-grade reliability. S3 serves as the persistent storage origin hosting static HTML, CSS, JavaScript bundles, images, and fonts. Amazon CloudFront: A global Content Delivery Network (CDN) service backed by hundreds of Edge Locations and regional edge caches worldwide. CloudFront terminates TLS connections, caches static content in close geographic proximity to end-users to minimize latency, supports automated payload compression, and integrates seamlessly with AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) for free custom domain SSL certificates. When integrated: S3 provides resilient, persistent storage, while CloudFront provides global edge acceleration, transport security (HTTPS), and attack mitigation. The entire frontend operates at scale without maintaining server infrastructure.
2. Approach 1: S3 Static Website Hosting (Basic) This approach represents the simplest method to publish a static website to the Internet within minutes, suitable for rapid testing, academic coursework, and non-production demonstrations.
Step 1: Build the React Application Compile the frontend source code into production-ready static assets:
# Standard build command for Vite or Create React App npm run build Depending on the bundler, static output files are generated in either dist/ (Vite) or build/ (Create React App). Ensure that index.html resides at the top level of the build directory.
Step 2: Create S3 Bucket and Upload Static Assets Open the AWS Management Console and navigate to Amazon S3. Click Create bucket, specify a globally unique bucket name, and select the target AWS Region (e.g., ap-southeast-1 - Singapore). Once created, open the bucket, click Upload, and upload the entire contents of your build directory (dist/ or build/). Verify that index.html is located directly at the root of the bucket. Step 3: Enable Static Website Hosting Go to the bucket’s Properties tab $\rightarrow$ scroll to Static website hosting $\rightarrow$ click Edit. Select Enable and configure: Hosting type: Host a static website. Index document: index.html. Error document: index.html (acts as a basic fallback for client-side routing). Click Save changes. Step 4: Configure Public Read Permissions By default, S3 activates global public access blocks. To permit public reads through the S3 Website Endpoint:
Navigate to the Permissions tab $\rightarrow$ Block public access (bucket settings) $\rightarrow$ click Edit $\rightarrow$ uncheck Block all public access $\rightarrow$ click Save changes (type confirm). Scroll down to Bucket policy $\rightarrow$ click Edit and paste the following policy: { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "PublicReadGetObject", "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": "*", "Action": "s3:GetObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::<your-bucket-name>/*" } ] } (Replace <your-bucket-name> with your actual S3 bucket name).
Step 5: Test the Website S3 provides a Bucket website endpoint formatted as: http://<your-bucket-name>.s3-website-<region>.amazonaws.com Accessing this endpoint in a browser immediately displays the live application.
Limitations of Direct S3 Static Website Hosting Despite its simplicity, this approach contains fundamental deficiencies that preclude production deployment:
❌ Lack of Native HTTPS: S3 Website Endpoints exclusively serve plaintext HTTP. Installing custom SSL/TLS certificates directly on an S3 Website Endpoint is unsupported, generating “Not Secure” browser warnings. ❌ Expanded Attack Surface: The entire bucket must be made globally public (Principal: "*"), violating the core AWS security tenet of Least Privilege. ❌ Elevated Latency: Traffic originates from a single AWS Region, increasing round-trip time (RTT) for geographically dispersed users. ❌ Incompatibility with OAC: S3 Website Endpoints act as custom HTTP web servers and cannot be secured using CloudFront Origin Access Control (OAC). Consequently, direct S3 Website Hosting is strictly recommended for sandbox experimentation. Production applications should universally adopt Approach 2.
3. Approach 2: S3 Private Bucket + CloudFront + Origin Access Control (OAC) (Production Grade) This architecture aligns strictly with the AWS Well-Architected Framework: The S3 Bucket remains strictly private with all public access blocked. Only Amazon CloudFront is granted read permissions via cryptographic authentication using Origin Access Control (OAC).
Key Architectural Advantages: 🔒 Zero Public Exposure: S3 Block All Public Access remains active. Direct requests to S3 object URLs return an immediate 403 Access Denied. ⚡ Global Edge Acceleration: Traffic is terminated at the nearest CloudFront Edge Location, serving cached content with sub-20ms latency. 🛡️ Free Managed SSL/TLS: Enforces modern HTTPS via AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) with seamless support for custom domain names via Amazon Route 53. 🛡️ DDoS Mitigation: Native integration with AWS Shield Standard at Layer 3/4 and optional AWS WAF inspection at Layer 7. Step-by-Step Implementation: Step 1: Create a Private S3 Bucket Create a new Amazon S3 Bucket. Critical: Keep Block all public access = ON (AWS default). Do not add public bucket policies (Principal: "*"). Do not enable S3 Static Website Hosting. Upload all compiled assets from the dist/ directory to the root of the bucket. Step 2: Create CloudFront Distribution In the CloudFront Console, select Create distribution. Origin Configuration: Origin domain: Select your S3 bucket from the dropdown list. ⚠️ Critical Note: Choose the standard S3 REST API endpoint (<bucket>.s3.<region>.amazonaws.com). Never select the S3 Website Endpoint; OAC only supports REST API endpoints.
Origin access: Select Origin access control settings (recommended). Origin access control: Click Create new OAC, provide a descriptive name, and select Signing behavior: Sign requests (recommended). Default Cache Behavior: Viewer protocol policy: Select Redirect HTTP to HTTPS. Allowed HTTP methods: GET, HEAD. Cache policy: CachingOptimized (AWS managed policy for maximum cache hit ratio). Compress objects automatically: Select Yes (activates Gzip and Brotli compression). Settings: Default root object: Enter index.html. Click Create distribution. Step 3: Configure S3 Bucket Policy for CloudFront OAC OAC signs every request originating from CloudFront to S3 using AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4).
Upon distribution creation, CloudFront prompts you with a policy statement. Add this statement to your S3 bucket under Permissions $\rightarrow$ Bucket policy:
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AllowCloudFrontServicePrincipalReadOnly", "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "Service": "cloudfront.amazonaws.com" }, "Action": "s3:GetObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::<your-bucket-name>/*", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "AWS:SourceArn": "arn:aws:cloudfront::<your-account-id>:distribution/<your-distribution-id>" } } } ] } Key Security Constraints in the Policy:
Principal: Grants access specifically to the cloudfront.amazonaws.com service principal. Action: Restricts permissions strictly to read operations via s3:GetObject. Condition (AWS:SourceArn): The cornerstone of defense. Ensures that only your designated CloudFront Distribution ARN can read from the bucket, completely mitigating the Confused Deputy problem. Once deployed, access the application via your CloudFront domain: https://dxxxxxxxxxxxxx.cloudfront.net
Direct requests to S3 object URLs will return Access Denied, verifying that your storage tier is fully isolated.
4. Handling Single Page Application (SPA) Client-Side Routing The Root Cause A classic obstacle when deploying React applications to static object storage involves client-side routes such as /login, /dashboard, or /profile:
Internal navigations triggered via React Router link clicks succeed because routing is managed in browser memory by the JavaScript runtime. However, when a user refreshes the browser on /dashboard or pastes https://domain.com/dashboard directly into the address bar, the browser requests the literal object path /dashboard from CloudFront and S3. Because S3 is an object store without server-side rewriting mechanisms, it finds no matching object and responds with 403 Forbidden or 404 Not Found. Solution: CloudFront Custom Error Responses Navigate to your CloudFront Distribution $\rightarrow$ Error pages tab $\rightarrow$ click Create custom error response. Handle HTTP 403 Forbidden: HTTP Error Code: 403: Forbidden. Customize error response: Yes. Response Page Path: /index.html. HTTP Response Code: 200: OK. Handle HTTP 404 Not Found: Repeat the identical configuration for 404: Not Found $\rightarrow$ Map to /index.html with HTTP Code 200: OK. Execution Lifecycle: When S3 signals an object miss (403/404), CloudFront intercepts the error and returns index.html accompanied by HTTP Status 200. The browser downloads index.html, executes the React bundle, and React Router inspects window.location.pathname to render the correct view seamlessly.
5. Performance Optimization & Cost Governance Best Practices 5.1. Strategic Cache-Control Headers Avoid homogenous cache durations across all static resources:
Hashed Bundles (index.a8f9b2.js, style.7c3e1a.css): Because asset contents are immutably tied to the cryptographic file hash, configure maximum caching (1 year): Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable HTML Entry Point (index.html): The entry HTML file links to current bundle hashes and must never be permanently cached by client browsers: Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate This guarantees that subsequent deployments are immediately visible upon browser reload without stale bundle conflicts. 5.2. Cost-Effective Cache Invalidation Following a deployment, CloudFront edge caches must be notified of updates:
Avoid global wildcard invalidations (/*), which rapidly consume AWS’s monthly tier of 1,000 free invalidation paths: # Avoid indiscriminate wildcard invalidations aws cloudfront create-invalidation --distribution-id <ID> --paths "/*" Target strictly index.html: # Best Practice: Invalidate only the entry file aws cloudfront create-invalidation --distribution-id <ID> --paths "/index.html" Because updated JS/CSS bundles feature unique hash names, updating index.html naturally forces browsers to fetch new assets. 5.3. Enable Automated Compression (Brotli & Gzip) Ensure Compress objects automatically = Yes is enabled on the CloudFront Cache Behavior. CloudFront dynamically compresses eligible text payloads (HTML, CSS, JS, JSON, SVG) using Brotli or Gzip, reducing network bandwidth by 60% to 80% and accelerating page loads for mobile clients.
5.4. Proactive Monitoring via AWS Budgets While S3 and CloudFront are remarkably cost-effective, configure monitoring to protect against unexpected traffic surges or crawler loops:
Establish an AWS Budget with an alert threshold (e.g., $5.00/month). Configure automated notifications via Amazon SNS or Email when forecasted or actual spend exceeds 80% of target limits. 6. Conclusion The architectural pairing of Amazon S3 Private Bucket with Amazon CloudFront and Origin Access Control (OAC) provides an industry-standard, production-ready foundation for modern web frontends:
Development & Lab Sandbox: Use S3 Static Website Hosting for rapid proof-of-concept testing. Production Environments: Mandate S3 Private Buckets secured with CloudFront OAC for enterprise-grade isolation. SPA Resilience: Configure CloudFront Custom Error Responses mapping 403/404 errors to /index.html. Operational Excellence: Implement differentiated Cache-Control policies, targeted invalidations, and AWS Budgets alerts. Week 1 Objectives: Get acquainted with the team, mentors, and the First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) development roadmap. Grasp core Cloud Computing fundamentals and the AWS Global Infrastructure (Regions, AZs, Edge Locations). Create and harden an AWS Free Tier account with AWS IAM following the Principle of Least Privilege. Install, configure AWS CLI v2, and gain hands-on proficiency with Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2). Tasks to be Carried Out This Week: Day Task 2 - Meet with FCAJ members and mentor.
- Review internship regulations, workplace culture, and the 12-week development roadmap.
- Setup development environment: VS Code, Git, and terminal utilities. 3 - Learn Cloud Computing foundations and cloud service models (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS).
- Study the AWS Shared Responsibility Model.
- Explore AWS Global Infrastructure: Regions, Availability Zones (AZs), and Edge Locations. 4 - Register an AWS Free Tier account and enable Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) on the Root Account.
- Study AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM): Users, Groups, Policies, and Roles.
- Create a dedicated IAM Admin user and enforce the Principle of Least Privilege. 5 - Install AWS CLI v2 on the local workstation.
- Configure Access Key ID, Secret Access Key, default region, and output format via aws configure.
- Execute essential CLI commands: verify caller identity (sts get-caller-identity), describe regions and instances. 6 - Study Amazon EC2 architecture: Instance Types (t2/t3.micro), AMIs, EBS storage, Key Pairs.
- Configure Security Groups restricting SSH (port 22) to trusted CIDR.
- Launch an Amazon Linux EC2 instance and establish a secure SSH session. Core Hands-on Lab & Practice: Secure AWS Account Hardening & Amazon EC2 Deployment In this foundational hands-on laboratory, I secured the AWS Root Account by activating Virtual MFA, constructed an IAM Admin Group with granular policies, and completely decommissioned root access keys. Subsequently, I configured AWS CLI v2 on the local environment and provisioned an Amazon Linux 2023 EC2 instance with an encrypted gp3 EBS volume, associated SSH Key Pairs, and validated remote terminal connectivity.
Key Achievements & Learning Outcomes: Mastered cloud delivery models and the AWS Shared Responsibility framework. Hardened the AWS Root account with MFA and implemented IAM best practices compliant with CIS benchmarks. Attained practical fluency in managing AWS infrastructure via both Management Console and AWS CLI v2. Successfully provisioned, configured, and remotely accessed Amazon EC2 virtual servers. Established a dependable engineering baseline for advanced cloud networking in Week 2.

title: Create a gateway endpoint
content:
Open the Amazon VPC console In the navigation pane, choose Endpoints, then click Create Endpoint: You will see 6 existing VPC endpoints that support AWS Systems Manager (SSM). These endpoints were deployed automatically by the CloudFormation Templates for this workshop.
In the Create endpoint console: Specify name of the endpoint: s3-gwe In service category, choose AWS services In Services, type s3 in the search box and choose the service with type gateway For VPC, select VPC Cloud from the drop-down. For Configure route tables, select the route table that is already associated with two subnets (note: this is not the main route table for the VPC, but a second route table created by CloudFormation). For Policy, leave the default option, Full Access, to allow full access to the service. You will deploy a VPC endpoint policy in a later lab module to demonstrate restricting access to S3 buckets based on policies. Do not add a tag to the VPC endpoint at this time. Click Create endpoint, then click x after receiving a successful creation message.

title: Introduction
content:
VPC endpoints VPC endpoints are virtual devices. They are horizontally scaled, redundant, and highly available VPC components. They allow communication between your compute resources and AWS services without imposing availability risks. Compute resources running in VPC can access Amazon S3 using a Gateway endpoint. PrivateLink interface endpoints can be used by compute resources running in VPC or on-premises. Workshop overview In this workshop, you will use two VPCs.
“VPC Cloud” is for cloud resources such as a Gateway endpoint and an EC2 instance to test with. “VPC On-Prem” simulates an on-premises environment such as a factory or corporate datacenter. An EC2 instance running strongSwan VPN software has been deployed in “VPC On-prem” and automatically configured to establish a Site-to-Site VPN tunnel with AWS Transit Gateway. This VPN simulates connectivity from an on-premises location to the AWS cloud. To minimize costs, only one VPN instance is provisioned to support this workshop. When planning VPN connectivity for your production workloads, AWS recommends using multiple VPN devices for high availability.

title: Blog 2: Deploying Docker on Amazon ECS & AWS Fargate
content:
Deploying Docker Applications on AWS with Amazon ECS and AWS Fargate 🔗 Published on AWS Study Group Community: View original Facebook post
Containerization with Docker has established itself as the gold standard in modern software engineering. It packages application source code, system binaries, dependencies, and configuration files into an immutable image, ensuring complete consistency from a developer’s local laptop to staging and production environments.
However, when deploying applications to the cloud, executing a simple docker run command solves only a fraction of the operational challenge. A production-ready enterprise system demands comprehensive capabilities: automated container lifecycle management, resilient traffic distribution, granular access governance, real-time observability, and self-healing resilience.
On Amazon Web Services (AWS), the synergy between Amazon ECS (Elastic Container Service) and AWS Fargate offers a premier serverless container solution. Rather than provisioning and maintaining virtual machine fleets (Amazon EC2), patching operating systems, or managing Docker daemons, AWS Fargate allows engineers to focus strictly on application logic and container definitions, while AWS manages the entire compute infrastructure underneath.
1. Architectural Component Overview Operating an enterprise-grade containerized workload on AWS requires the orchestration of several integrated services:
Amazon ECR (Elastic Container Registry): A fully managed, highly available private Docker container registry integrated natively with AWS IAM. Once built, container images are pushed to ECR for versioned storage and automated image vulnerability scanning. Amazon ECS (Elastic Container Service): AWS’s cloud-native container orchestrator. ECS manages cluster workloads via three foundational abstractions: Task Definition: A declarative JSON blueprint specifying container configuration: container image URI from ECR, vCPU/RAM allocations, port mappings, environment variables, storage mounts, and IAM roles. Task: An active runtime execution instance (equivalent to a running container instance) instantiated from a Task Definition. Service: The controller responsible for maintaining the specified number of concurrent tasks (Desired Count), registering tasks with the load balancer, and coordinating zero-downtime rolling deployments. AWS Fargate: A serverless compute engine purpose-built for containers. Fargate dynamically allocates compute resources matching the exact vCPU and memory profiles specified in the Task Definition without requiring EC2 server administration. Application Load Balancer (ALB): A Layer 7 load balancer that serves as the single public entry point, terminating incoming HTTPS requests and intelligently distributing traffic across healthy Fargate tasks. Amazon CloudWatch: Provides centralized telemetry collection via CloudWatch Logs (/ecs/my-web-app) and performance metrics via Container Insights (vCPU, memory, and network utilization). AWS IAM (Identity and Access Management): Enforces granular privilege boundaries across the architecture through two distinct roles: the Task Execution Role and the Task Role. 2. Architecture Diagram & End-to-End Workflow The following architecture adheres strictly to the operational and security pillars of the AWS Well-Architected Framework:
Step-by-Step System Lifecycle: Step 0 - Build & Publish Image (docker push): The developer builds the container image locally or via an automated CI/CD pipeline, tags the release version, authenticates, and pushes the image to Amazon ECR. Step 1 - Public Ingress (HTTPS Request): Users submit requests via web browsers over HTTPS. Traffic arrives at the Application Load Balancer (ALB), which resides in Public Subnets distributed across two Availability Zones (AZs) for high availability. Step 2 - Routing to Private Targets (Forward to targets): The ALB performs continuous health checks and securely routes requests directly to the private IP addresses of the running Fargate Tasks located in Private Subnets. The ECS Service maintains Desired Count = 2, balancing Task A in AZ-1 and Task B in AZ-2. Step 3 - Image Pull & Provisioning (Pull Image): During task bootstrapping, Fargate invokes the Task Execution Role to authenticate against Amazon ECR and pull the container image through private VPC channels (via NAT Gateway or AWS PrivateLink VPC Endpoints). Step 4 - Telemetry & Log Streaming (Stream logs): Standard output and standard error streams generated by the container are shipped in real time to the designated CloudWatch Logs group (/ecs/my-web-app) for operational auditing and debugging. 3. Critical Engineering Considerations 3.1. Differentiating Task Execution Role vs. Task Role A frequent misconception among cloud engineers involves confusing the distinct security boundaries between these two IAM roles:
Dimension Task Execution Role Task Role Identity Entity Granted to the ECS Agent / Fargate Infrastructure Granted to the Application Code running inside the container Lifecycle Phase Invoked during task provisioning and container launch Active throughout the runtime duration of the application Typical Permissions - Pulling images from Amazon ECR (ecr:GetDownloadUrlFor...)
- Creating log streams and pushing events to CloudWatch Logs
- Fetching sensitive secrets from AWS Secrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store - Reading/writing objects in Amazon S3 buckets
- Querying database items in Amazon DynamoDB
- Publishing messages to Amazon SQS / Amazon SNS 🔒 Security Best Practice: Clear separation between these two roles strictly enforces the Principle of Least Privilege, preventing any compromised application container from abusing infrastructure-level provisioning permissions.
3.2. awsvpc Networking Mode & Defense-in-Depth Security Mandatory awsvpc Networking: AWS Fargate mandates the awsvpc network mode. Each Fargate task is allocated a dedicated Elastic Network Interface (ENI) with a private IP address within the VPC’s subnet range, granting tasks parity with native EC2 instances. ALB Target Group Type: Because tasks receive individual private IP addresses, the associated ALB Target Group must be configured with Target type = IP (rather than Instance). Security Group Chaining: ALB Security Group: Permits inbound HTTP/HTTPS traffic (ports 80/443) from the public Internet (0.0.0.0/0). Fargate Task Security Group: Isolated within Private Subnets without direct public routability. The inbound rule exclusively permits traffic originating from the ALB Security Group on the containerized application port (e.g., port 3000, 8080). Private Egress Connectivity: To allow tasks in private subnets to pull container images from ECR and stream logs to CloudWatch, subnets require egress routes via a NAT Gateway or, preferably, dedicated VPC Endpoints (AWS PrivateLink). 3.3. Zero-Downtime Rolling Updates & Circuit Breakers Amazon ECS natively orchestrates zero-downtime rolling updates coordinated with ALB health monitoring:
When a new image tag is deployed, ECS provisions new Fargate tasks alongside existing active tasks. The ALB initiates health check requests (e.g., /health) against newly launched tasks. Once new tasks transition to healthy, the ALB begins shifting live traffic to them. The ALB applies Deregistration Delay (Connection Draining), allowing in-flight requests on older tasks to complete gracefully before stopping them. Deployment Circuit Breaker: When enabled, if new tasks repeatedly fail health checks or crash loop, ECS automatically aborts the deployment and triggers an immediate Rollback to the previously stable version, preventing outages. 4. Operational Monitoring & Cost Optimization 4.1. Live Observability & Remote Debugging with ECS Exec CloudWatch Container Insights: Delivers real-time diagnostic dashboards visualizing vCPU utilization, memory saturation, network throughput, and task counts. AWS ECS Exec: Enables developers to execute interactive shell sessions directly inside a running Fargate container without opening SSH port 22, managing SSH keypairs, or configuring bastion hosts. Communications are securely tunneled over AWS Systems Manager (SSM) protocols. 4.2. Practical Cloud Cost Management While Fargate eliminates server maintenance overhead, compute and networking components must be managed judiciously:
Adopt AWS Fargate Spot: For stateless web workers, batch processing, or non-production staging environments, Fargate Spot provides up to 70% cost savings compared to standard On-Demand Fargate pricing. VPC Endpoints vs. NAT Gateway: NAT Gateways incur hourly availability charges in addition to per-GB data processing fees. For frequent, large image pulls, provisioning Interface VPC Endpoints for ECR (ecr.api, ecr.dkr) and a Gateway VPC Endpoint for S3 substantially eliminates recurring NAT data processing expenses. Automated Budget Alerts: Implement AWS Budgets to enforce monthly spending targets for the ECS cluster and receive proactive alerts via Email or SNS whenever actual or forecasted spend crosses 80%. 5. Conclusion Deploying containerized applications on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate delivers exceptional operational agility and cloud resilience:
Serverless Compute: Fully abstracts host instance provisioning, AMI lifecycle maintenance, and OS security patching. High Availability by Default: Multi-AZ distribution ensures fault tolerance and automatic recovery across availability zones. Layered Defense: Decoupled public ingress (ALB) and private execution environments (Fargate) combined with strict IAM role boundaries. Enterprise CI/CD Integration: Integrates seamlessly with AWS CodePipeline or GitHub Actions, establishing an enterprise-ready foundation for scalable cloud workloads. Week 2 Objectives: Master cloud network architecture using Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC). Design IP address schemas using CIDR blocks and implement Public/Private subnet separation. Configure routing tables with Internet Gateways (IGW) and NAT Gateways for secure egress. Implement defense-in-depth network access control using Security Groups (Stateful) and NACLs (Stateless). Tasks to be Carried Out This Week: Day Task 2 - Study Amazon VPC architecture, RFC 1918 private IP spaces, and CIDR subnetting (10.0.0.0/16).
- Differentiate Public and Private Subnets across Multi-Availability Zones for High Availability.

- Design Public Subnet Route Tables enabling Internet-facing traffic.

- Configure granular Inbound/Outbound rules for HTTP (80), HTTPS (443), and SSH (22). 5 - Study Elastic IP (EIP) addresses and Elastic Network Interfaces (ENI).
- Associate and reallocate EIPs seamlessly between instances for failover resilience.
- Review billing implications of unattached idle Elastic IPs. 6 - Comprehensive Practice: Build a custom 2-Tier VPC spanned across 2 Availability Zones.
- Deploy a Bastion Host in the Public Subnet and an isolated workload in the Private Subnet.
- Verify Bastion SSH tunneling and validate outbound package updates via NAT Gateway. Core Hands-on Lab & Practice: Designing & Deploying a Multi-Tier Production-Ready Custom VPC In this hands-on lab, I architected a custom VPC (10.0.0.0/16) comprising two Public Subnets and two Private Subnets across dual Availability Zones. The architecture incorporated an Internet Gateway for public ingress/egress and an allocated NAT Gateway routing private outbound connections. Workloads in private subnets were verified to have zero direct internet exposure, accessible strictly via an encrypted Bastion Host tunnel.
Key Achievements & Learning Outcomes: Architected an enterprise-grade VPC with resilient Multi-AZ topology and clean subnet segmentation. Configured end-to-end routing incorporating Internet Gateways, NAT Gateways, and isolated Route Tables. Implemented rigorous multi-layered filtering combining Stateful Security Groups and Stateless NACLs. Gained practical expertise in deploying Bastion Host jump boxes for secure administrative access. Developed acute troubleshooting skills for resolving network routing and CIDR overlap bottlenecks.

title: Proposal
content:
⚠️ Note: The information below is for reference purposes only. Please do not copy verbatim for your report, including this warning.
In this section, you need to summarize the contents of the workshop that you plan to conduct.
IoT Weather Platform for Lab Research A Unified AWS Serverless Solution for Real-Time Weather Monitoring 1. Executive Summary The IoT Weather Platform is designed for the ITea Lab team in Ho Chi Minh City to enhance weather data collection and analysis. It supports up to 5 weather stations, with potential scalability to 10-15, utilizing Raspberry Pi edge devices with ESP32 sensors to transmit data via MQTT. The platform leverages AWS Serverless services to deliver real-time monitoring, predictive analytics, and cost efficiency, with access restricted to 5 lab members via Amazon Cognito.
2. Problem Statement What’s the Problem? Current weather stations require manual data collection, becoming unmanageable with multiple units. There is no centralized system for real-time data or analytics, and third-party platforms are costly and overly complex.
The Solution The platform uses AWS IoT Core to ingest MQTT data, AWS Lambda and API Gateway for processing, Amazon S3 for storage (including a data lake), and AWS Glue Crawlers and ETL jobs to extract, transform, and load data from the S3 data lake to another S3 bucket for analysis. AWS Amplify with Next.js provides the web interface, and Amazon Cognito ensures secure access. Similar to Thingsboard and CoreIoT, users can register new devices and manage connections, though this platform operates on a smaller scale and is designed for private use. Key features include real-time dashboards, trend analysis, and low operational costs.
Benefits and Return on Investment The solution establishes a foundational resource for lab members to develop a larger IoT platform, serving as a study resource, and provides a data foundation for AI enthusiasts for model training or analysis. It reduces manual reporting for each station via a centralized platform, simplifying management and maintenance, and improves data reliability. Monthly costs are $0.66 USD per the AWS Pricing Calculator, with a 12-month total of $7.92 USD. All IoT equipment costs are covered by the existing weather station setup, eliminating additional development expenses. The break-even period of 6-12 months is achieved through significant time savings from reduced manual work.
3. Solution Architecture The platform employs a serverless AWS architecture to manage data from 5 Raspberry Pi-based stations, scalable to 15. Data is ingested via AWS IoT Core, stored in an S3 data lake, and processed by AWS Glue Crawlers and ETL jobs to transform and load it into another S3 bucket for analysis. Lambda and API Gateway handle additional processing, while Amplify with Next.js hosts the dashboard, secured by Cognito. The architecture is detailed below:
AWS Services Used AWS IoT Core: Ingests MQTT data from 5 stations, scalable to 15. AWS Lambda: Processes data and triggers Glue jobs (two functions). Amazon API Gateway: Facilitates web app communication. Amazon S3: Stores raw data in a data lake and processed outputs (two buckets). AWS Glue: Crawlers catalog data, and ETL jobs transform and load it. AWS Amplify: Hosts the Next.js web interface. Amazon Cognito: Secures access for lab users. Component Design Edge Devices: Raspberry Pi collects and filters sensor data, sending it to IoT Core. Data Ingestion: AWS IoT Core receives MQTT messages from the edge devices. Data Storage: Raw data is stored in an S3 data lake; processed data is stored in another S3 bucket. Data Processing: AWS Glue Crawlers catalog the data, and ETL jobs transform it for analysis. Web Interface: AWS Amplify hosts a Next.js app for real-time dashboards and analytics. User Management: Amazon Cognito manages user access, allowing up to 5 active accounts. 4. Technical Implementation Implementation Phases This project has two parts—setting up weather edge stations and building the weather platform—each following 4 phases:
Build Theory and Draw Architecture: Research Raspberry Pi setup with ESP32 sensors and design the AWS serverless architecture (1 month pre-internship) Calculate Price and Check Practicality: Use AWS Pricing Calculator to estimate costs and adjust if needed (Month 1). Fix Architecture for Cost or Solution Fit: Tweak the design (e.g., optimize Lambda with Next.js) to stay cost-effective and usable (Month 2). Develop, Test, and Deploy: Code the Raspberry Pi setup, AWS services with CDK/SDK, and Next.js app, then test and release to production (Months 2-3). Technical Requirements
Weather Edge Station: Sensors (temperature, humidity, rainfall, wind speed), a microcontroller (ESP32), and a Raspberry Pi as the edge device. Raspberry Pi runs Raspbian, handles Docker for filtering, and sends 1 MB/day per station via MQTT over Wi-Fi. Weather Platform: Practical knowledge of AWS Amplify (hosting Next.js), Lambda (minimal use due to Next.js), AWS Glue (ETL), S3 (two buckets), IoT Core (gateway and rules), and Cognito (5 users). Use AWS CDK/SDK to code interactions (e.g., IoT Core rules to S3). Next.js reduces Lambda workload for the fullstack web app. 5. Timeline & Milestones Project Timeline
Pre-Internship (Month 0): 1 month for planning and old station review. Internship (Months 1-3): 3 months. Month 1: Study AWS and upgrade hardware. Month 2: Design and adjust architecture. Month 3: Implement, test, and launch. Post-Launch: Up to 1 year for research. 6. Budget Estimation You can find the budget estimation on the AWS Pricing Calculator.
Or you can download the Budget Estimation File.
Infrastructure Costs AWS Services: AWS Lambda: $0.00/month (1,000 requests, 512 MB storage). S3 Standard: $0.15/month (6 GB, 2,100 requests, 1 GB scanned). Data Transfer: $0.02/month (1 GB inbound, 1 GB outbound). AWS Amplify: $0.35/month (256 MB, 500 ms requests). Amazon API Gateway: $0.01/month (2,000 requests). AWS Glue ETL Jobs: $0.02/month (2 DPUs). AWS Glue Crawlers: $0.07/month (1 crawler). MQTT (IoT Core): $0.08/month (5 devices, 45,000 messages). Total: $0.7/month, $8.40/12 months
Hardware: $265 one-time (Raspberry Pi 5 and sensors). 7. Risk Assessment Risk Matrix Network Outages: Medium impact, medium probability. Sensor Failures: High impact, low probability. Cost Overruns: Medium impact, low probability. Mitigation Strategies Network: Local storage on Raspberry Pi with Docker. Sensors: Regular checks and spares. Cost: AWS budget alerts and optimization. Contingency Plans Revert to manual methods if AWS fails. Use CloudFormation for cost-related rollbacks. 8. Expected Outcomes Technical Improvements: Real-time data and analytics replace manual processes.
Scalable to 10-15 stations.
Long-term Value 1-year data foundation for AI research.
Reusable for future projects.

title: Blog 3: Building a Serverless REST API with Lambda, API Gateway & DynamoDB
content:
Building a Serverless REST API with AWS Lambda, Amazon API Gateway, and Amazon DynamoDB 🔗 Published on AWS Study Group Community: View original Facebook post
In traditional backend architectures, web applications rely on persistent virtual servers (such as VPS or Amazon EC2) that run 24/7 to listen for and process client HTTP requests. This model imposes continuous operational burdens: operating system patch management, capacity planning, Auto Scaling configuration, and ongoing infrastructure costs even when the system experiences zero user traffic.
The advent of the Serverless Architecture paradigm has revolutionized cloud-native backend development. Rather than provisioning and managing server instances, software engineers can dedicate 100% of their focus to core business logic. All underlying infrastructure provisioning, high-availability multi-AZ deployment, automatic scaling during unpredictable traffic spikes, and scaling down to zero during idle periods are handled natively by the cloud provider.
The canonical serverless trio—Amazon API Gateway + AWS Lambda + Amazon DynamoDB—represents the industry-standard architecture for building robust, scalable CRUD (Create, Read, Update, Delete) REST APIs with minimal maintenance overhead and pay-as-you-go cost efficiency.
1. Architectural Component Overview The system is constructed entirely using AWS fully managed, serverless services:
Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API): A managed, distributed entry point that accepts inbound HTTP/HTTPS requests from clients (browsers, mobile applications, or CLI tools). API Gateway manages rate limiting, handles route parsing based on HTTP method and path, and directly integrates with backend compute engines. AWS Lambda (CRUD Handler): An event-driven serverless compute service. Lambda provisions runtime execution environments only upon receiving requests forwarded by API Gateway, dynamically scales concurrent executions to match incoming demand, and terminates immediately after execution, eliminating idle server expenses. Amazon DynamoDB (Items Table): A fully managed NoSQL key-value and document database delivering consistent, single-digit millisecond latency at any scale with automated Multi-AZ data replication. AWS IAM (Execution Role): Manages identity and provides short-lived temporary security credentials to the Lambda function. Through this execution role, Lambda accesses DynamoDB and streams logs to CloudWatch without embedding static Access Keys or Secret Keys in the application code. Amazon CloudWatch Logs: Centralizes the capture, indexing, and storage of runtime execution logs, invocation metrics, and unhandled exceptions for operational monitoring and debugging. 2. Architecture Diagram & Request Lifecycle The following diagram illustrates the end-to-end request lifecycle of the Serverless REST API:
Step-by-Step Request Execution Workflow: Step 1 - Inbound Request (HTTPS Request): The client (React SPA, mobile client, or Postman) initiates an HTTPS request to the public Invoke URL provided by Amazon API Gateway. Step 2 - Intelligent Routing (Route to Lambda integration): API Gateway analyzes the HTTP method (GET, PUT, DELETE) and path (/items, /items/{id}), formats the event payload (Payload Format Version 2.0), and triggers the AWS Lambda function via Lambda Proxy Integration. Step 3 - Business Logic & NoSQL Query (Read/Write items via AWS SDK): The Lambda function parses the incoming event, extracts Path Parameters or the JSON Request Body, and uses the AWS SDK for JavaScript v3 to perform the corresponding CRUD operation against the Amazon DynamoDB table (http-crud-tutorial-items). Step 4 - Telemetry & Log Ingestion (Write logs): During invocation, runtime performance statistics, application console.log statements, and memory metrics are automatically streamed to CloudWatch Logs. Step 5 - Structured Response to Client: Lambda compiles a standard HTTP response object (containing statusCode: 200, headers: {"Content-Type": "application/json"}, and a serialized JSON body) and returns it to API Gateway, which forwards the response back to the client. 3. Implementing the CRUD REST Service 3.1. Database Design with Amazon DynamoDB Table Name: http-crud-tutorial-items. Partition Key: id (Type: String) serving as the unique identifier for each item. Capacity Mode: On-Demand (PAY_PER_REQUEST). Under On-Demand billing, you do not pre-provision Read/Write Capacity Units (RCU/WCU). DynamoDB instantly accommodates arbitrary workloads and charges strictly per read/write request, ideal for unpredictable traffic patterns. 3.2. Business Logic Implementation on AWS Lambda (Node.js) Using the Node.js 20.x runtime and the modular AWS SDK v3 (@aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb with DynamoDBDocumentClient to simplify native JavaScript object mapping):
import { DynamoDBClient } from "@aws-sdk/client-dynamodb"; import { DynamoDBDocumentClient, ScanCommand, PutCommand, GetCommand, DeleteCommand, } from "@aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb"; const client = new DynamoDBClient({}); const dynamo = DynamoDBDocumentClient.from(client); const tableName = "http-crud-tutorial-items"; export const handler = async (event, context) => { let body; let statusCode = 200; const headers = { "Content-Type": "application/json", }; try { const routeKey = `${event.requestContext.http.method} ${event.requestContext.http.path}`; switch (routeKey) { // 1. DELETE /items/{id} - Delete record by ID case `DELETE /items/${event.pathParameters?.id}`: await dynamo.send( new DeleteCommand({ TableName: tableName, Key: { id: event.pathParameters.id }, }) ); body = JSON.stringify({ message: `Deleted item ${event.pathParameters.id}` }); break; // 2. GET /items/{id} - Retrieve record details by ID case `GET /items/${event.pathParameters?.id}`: const getRes = await dynamo.send( new GetCommand({ TableName: tableName, Key: { id: event.pathParameters.id }, }) ); body = JSON.stringify(getRes.Item || {}); break; // 3. GET /items - Retrieve all records case "GET /items": const scanRes = await dynamo.send( new ScanCommand({ TableName: tableName }) ); body = JSON.stringify(scanRes.Items || []); break; // 4. PUT /items - Create or update record case "PUT /items": const requestJSON = JSON.parse(event.body); await dynamo.send( new PutCommand({ TableName: tableName, Item: { id: requestJSON.id, price: requestJSON.price, name: requestJSON.name, updatedAt: new Date().toISOString(), }, }) ); body = JSON.stringify({ message: `Put item ${requestJSON.id}` }); break; default: throw new Error(`Unsupported route: "${routeKey}"`); } } catch (err) { statusCode = 400; body = JSON.stringify({ error: err.message }); } return { statusCode, body, headers, }; }; Configuring the IAM Execution Role: Adhering to the Principle of Least Privilege, restrict access strictly to the target table ARN:
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "dynamodb:GetItem", "dynamodb:PutItem", "dynamodb:DeleteItem", "dynamodb:Scan" ], "Resource": "arn:aws:dynamodb:<region>:<account-id>:table/http-crud-tutorial-items" } ] } 3.3. Route Mapping in Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API) Configure four discrete routes in API Gateway and attach them to a single Lambda Proxy Integration:
GET /items $\rightarrow$ Lists all items. GET /items/{id} $\rightarrow$ Fetches a single item via the {id} path parameter. PUT /items $\rightarrow$ Creates or updates an item from the JSON request body. DELETE /items/{id} $\rightarrow$ Removes an item matching {id}. 3.4. API Verification with cURL / Postman Upon deployment, API Gateway yields an Invoke URL structured as: https://<api-id>.execute-api.<region>.amazonaws.com. Verify each operation using standard HTTP tooling:
Create: curl -X PUT "https://<api-url>/items" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"id": "item-01", "name": "Mechanical Keyboard", "price": 120}' Read List: curl -X GET "https://<api-url>/items" Read Details: curl -X GET "https://<api-url>/items/item-01" Delete: curl -X DELETE "https://<api-url>/items/item-01" 4. Architectural Analysis: HTTP API vs. REST API Amazon API Gateway provides two primary RESTful choices. Selecting the appropriate API type aligns architectural complexity with business requirements:
Evaluation Dimension HTTP API (Recommended for Serverless) REST API (Traditional Enterprise) Pricing Ultra Cost-Effective: $1.00 per million requests (up to ~70% cost savings). Higher: $3.50 per million requests. Latency Significantly lower overhead engineered specifically for Lambda proxying. Slightly higher due to multiple transformation middleware layers. Authentication Native support for OIDC and JWT Authorizers (Cognito, Auth0). Supports Cognito User Pools, Lambda Authorizers, API Keys, and IAM. Quota & Throttling Basic Stage-level throttling. Advanced Usage Plans and API Keys tailored for API monetization (SaaS). Advanced Features No native request schema validation or caching. Comprehensive: Built-in response caching, payload transformations, AWS WAF, Private Endpoints. 💡 Architectural Recommendation: Choose HTTP APIs for standard web and mobile backends requiring low latency, serverless cost optimization, and JWT security. Reserve REST APIs for scenarios requiring granular API Key monetization or API Gateway-level response caching.
5. Engineering Best Practices & Production Hardening Beware of DynamoDB Scan Operations at Scale: A Scan sequentially parses every item across the entire physical dataset. As tables grow to millions of rows, Scan operations degrade latency, exhaust Read Capacity Units (RCUs), and escalate costs. Production workloads should universally favor Query operations executed against the Partition Key, Sort Key, or secondary indexes (Global Secondary Indexes - GSI). Configure Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS): When client web applications (React/Vue) hosted on external domains consume the API, enable CORS in API Gateway settings, permitting approved headers (Content-Type, Authorization) and HTTP methods (GET, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS). Cold Start Optimization: To minimize initial Lambda invocation latency: Leverage AWS SDK v3 and import only the required client libraries (@aws-sdk/client-dynamodb) rather than the monolithic SDK. Initialize database clients outside the execution handler to enable TCP connection reuse across warm invocations. Resilient Input Validation & HTTP Status Discipline: Wrap execution blocks in robust try...catch structures and return canonical REST status codes: 400 Bad Request: Missing mandatory parameters or invalid JSON. 404 Not Found: Targeted identifier does not exist. 500 Internal Server Error: Unhandled database or runtime exceptions. Infrastructure as Code (IaC): For enterprise lifecycles, declare all components programmatically using AWS SAM (Serverless Application Model) or AWS CDK to enable reproducible CI/CD pipelines across environments. 6. Cost Governance & Resource Cleanup Serverless architecture offers exceptional cost efficiency for early-stage and medium workloads through generous AWS Free Tier allocations:
AWS Lambda: 1,000,000 requests per month free perpetually, plus 3.2 million seconds of compute time. Amazon DynamoDB: 25 GB of persistent storage free perpetually, accompanied by 25 write capacity units and 25 read capacity units. Amazon API Gateway: 1,000,000 API calls per month free during the initial 12-month tier. ⚠️ Resource Teardown: Upon completing laboratory testing, delete temporary DynamoDB tables, API Gateway stages, and CloudWatch log groups to ensure your account incurs zero ongoing residual charges.
7. Conclusion The combination of Amazon API Gateway + AWS Lambda + Amazon DynamoDB demonstrates the core strengths of cloud-native serverless backends:
Zero Infrastructure Overhead: Eliminates operating system administration, capacity provisioning, and server patch cycles. Elastic Autoscaling: Seamlessly scales from zero requests to tens of thousands of requests per second without operational intervention. Pay-per-Execution Economics: Costs scale strictly with active user invocations, delivering unprecedented financial efficiency. title: Access S3 from on-premises
content:
Overview In this section, you will create an Interface endpoint to access Amazon S3 from a simulated on-premises environment. The Interface endpoint will allow you to route to Amazon S3 over a VPN connection from your simulated on-premises environment.
Why using Interface endpoint:
Gateway endpoints only work with resources running in the VPC where they are created. Interface endpoints work with resources running in VPC, and also resources running in on-premises environments. Connectivty from your on-premises environment to the cloud can be provided by AWS Site-to-Site VPN or AWS Direct Connect. Interface endpoints allow you to connect to services powered by AWS PrivateLink. These services include some AWS services, services hosted by other AWS customers and partners in their own VPCs (referred to as PrivateLink Endpoint Services), and supported AWS Marketplace Partner services. For this workshop, we will focus on connecting to Amazon S3.

title: On-premises DNS Simulation
content:
AWS PrivateLink endpoints have a fixed IP address in each Availability Zone where they are deployed, for the life of the endpoint (until it is deleted). These IP addresses are attached to Elastic Network Interfaces (ENIs). AWS recommends using DNS to resolve the IP addresses for endpoints so that downstream applications use the latest IP addresses when ENIs are added to new AZs, or deleted over time.
In this section, you will create a forwarding rule to send DNS resolution requests from a simulated on-premises environment to a Route 53 Private Hosted Zone. This section leverages the infrastructure deployed by CloudFormation in the Prepare the environment section.
Create DNS Alias Records for the Interface endpoint Navigate to the Route 53 management console (Hosted Zones section). The CloudFormation template you deployed in the Prepare the environment section created this Private Hosted Zone. Click on the name of the Private Hosted Zone, s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com: Create a new record in the Private Hosted Zone: Record name and record type keep default options Alias Button: Click to enable Route traffic to: Alias to VPC Endpoint Region: US East (N. Virginia) [us-east-1] Choose endpoint: Paste the Regional VPC Endpoint DNS name from your text editor (you saved when doing section 4.3) Click Add another record, and add a second record using the following values. Click Create records when finished to create both records. Record name: *. Record type: keep default value (type A) Alias Button: Click to enable Route traffic to: Alias to VPC Endpoint Region: US East (N. Virginia) [us-east-1] Choose endpoint: Paste the Regional VPC Endpoint DNS name from your text editor The new records appear in the Route 53 console:
Create a Resolver Forwarding Rule Route 53 Resolver Forwarding Rules allow you to forward DNS queries from your VPC to other sources for name resolution. Outside of a workshop environment, you might use this feature to forward DNS queries from your VPC to DNS servers running on-premises. In this section, you will simulate an on-premises conditional forwarder by creating a forwarding rule that forwards DNS queries for Amazon S3 to a Private Hosted Zone running in “VPC Cloud” in-order to resolve the PrivateLink interface endpoint regional DNS name.
From the Route 53 management console, click Inbound endpoints on the left side bar In the Inbound endpoints console, click the ID of the inbound endpoint Copy the two IP addresses listed to your text editor From the Route 53 menu, choose Resolver > Rules, and click Create rule: In the Create rule console: Name: myS3Rule Rule type: Forward Domain name: s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com VPC: VPC On-prem Outbound endpoint: VPCOnpremOutboundEndpoint Target IP Addresses: Enter both IP addresses from your text editor (inbound endpoint addresses) and then click Submit You have successfully created resolver forwarding rule.
Test the on-premises DNS Simulation Connect to Test-Interface-Endpoint EC2 instance with Session manager Test DNS resolution. The dig command will return the IP addresses assigned to the VPC Interface endpoint running in VPC Cloud (your IP’s will be different): dig +short s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com The IP addresses returned are the VPC endpoint IP addresses, NOT the Resolver IP addresses you pasted from your text editor. The IP addresses of the Resolver endpoint and the VPC endpoint look similar because they are all from the VPC Cloud CIDR block.
Navigate to the VPC menu (Endpoints section), select the S3 Interface endpoint. Click the Subnets tab and verify that the IP addresses returned by Dig match the VPC endpoint: Return to your shell and use the AWS CLI to test listing your S3 buckets: aws s3 ls --endpoint-url https://s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com Terminate your Session Manager session: In this section you created an Interface endpoint for Amazon S3. This endpoint can be reached from on-premises through Site-to-Site VPN or AWS Direct Connect. Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoints simulated forwarding DNS requests from on-premises to a Private Hosted Zone running the cloud. Route 53 inbound Endpoints recieved the resolution request and returned a response containing the IP addresses of the VPC interface endpoint. Using DNS to resolve the endpoint IP addresses provides high availability in-case of an Availability Zone outage.

title: VPC Endpoint Policies
content:
When you create an interface or gateway endpoint, you can attach an endpoint policy to it that controls access to the service to which you are connecting. A VPC endpoint policy is an IAM resource policy that you attach to an endpoint. If you do not attach a policy when you create an endpoint, AWS attaches a default policy for you that allows full access to the service through the endpoint.
You can create a policy that restricts access to specific S3 buckets only. This is useful if you only want certain S3 Buckets to be accessible through the endpoint.
In this section you will create a VPC endpoint policy that restricts access to the S3 bucket specified in the VPC endpoint policy.
Connect to an EC2 instance and verify connectivity to S3 Start a new AWS Session Manager session on the instance named Test-Gateway-Endpoint. From the session, verify that you can list the contents of the bucket you created in Part 1: Access S3 from VPC: aws s3 ls s3://\<your-bucket-name\> The bucket contents include the two 1 GB files uploaded in earlier.
Create a new S3 bucket; follow the naming pattern you used in Part 1, but add a ‘-2’ to the name. Leave other fields as default and click create Successfully create bucket
Navigate to: Services > VPC > Endpoints, then select the Gateway VPC endpoint you created earlier. Click the Policy tab. Click Edit policy. The default policy allows access to all S3 Buckets through the VPC endpoint.
In Edit Policy console, copy & Paste the following policy, then replace yourbucketname-2 with your 2nd bucket name. This policy will allow access through the VPC endpoint to your new bucket, but not any other bucket in Amazon S3. Secure Hybrid Access to S3 using VPC Endpoints Overview AWS PrivateLink provides private connectivity to AWS services from VPCs and your on-premises networks, without exposing your traffic to the Public Internet.
In this lab, you will learn how to create, configure, and test VPC endpoints that enable your workloads to reach AWS services without traversing the Public Internet.
You will create two types of endpoints to access Amazon S3: a Gateway VPC endpoint, and an Interface VPC endpoint. These two types of VPC endpoints offer different benefits depending on if you are accessing Amazon S3 from the cloud or your on-premises location
Gateway - Create a gateway endpoint to send traffic to Amazon S3 or DynamoDB using private IP addresses.You route traffic from your VPC to the gateway endpoint using route tables. Interface - Create an interface endpoint to send traffic to endpoint services that use a Network Load Balancer to distribute traffic. Traffic destined for the endpoint service is resolved using DNS.
